title: AES, the modern standard
syllabusUnit: Unit II: Advanced Encryption Standard & Rijndael
covers: AES structure, 4 round steps, key expansion, finite field GF(2^8) in plain words
learningGoals: You will be able to describe the 4x4 State Matrix of AES.
You will be able to explain the 4 transformations: SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey.
You will be able to state the key sizes and round counts for AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256.

lessonCards.title: The 4x4 State Matrix
lessonCards.analogy: A 16-seat auditorium arranged in a 4-by-4 grid where 128 bits sit as 16 individual bytes.
lessonCards.coreConcept: AES (Rijndael) processes 128-bit blocks organized as a 4x4 matrix of bytes: 16 bytes = 128 bits. Unlike DES, AES is a substitution-permutation network, not a Feistel cipher.
lessonCards.example: Every round transforms all 16 bytes simultaneously across rows and columns.

lessonCards.title: The 4 AES Transformations
lessonCards.analogy: 1. Swap cards (SubBytes), 2. Slide rows (ShiftRows), 3. Mix blenders (MixColumns), 4. Stamp secret key (AddRoundKey).
lessonCards.coreConcept: SubBytes provides non-linear confusion via an S-box in GF(2^8). ShiftRows slides rows cyclically. MixColumns multiplies columns by a fixed matrix. AddRoundKey XORs round subkeys.
lessonCards.example: The final round omits MixColumns to allow symmetric reverse decryption.

lessonCards.title: Key Sizes & Round Counts
lessonCards.analogy: Longer keys require more rounds of mixing: 10 rounds for 128-bit, 12 rounds for 192-bit, 14 rounds for 256-bit.
lessonCards.coreConcept: AES-128 uses 10 rounds; AES-192 uses 12 rounds; AES-256 uses 14 rounds. Even with the fastest supercomputers, brute-forcing AES-128 would take billions of years.
lessonCards.example: AES-256 is certified by NSA for top-secret classified government communication.

questions.prompt: What is the block size processed by the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)?
questions.explanation: AES strictly operates on 128-bit blocks (arranged as a 4x4 byte state matrix), regardless of whether key length is 128, 192, or 256 bits.
wrongExplanations: Correct! AES block size is always 128 bits.
64 bits was the legacy DES block size.
256 bits is a possible AES key length, but block size remains 128.
512 bits is used in SHA-512 hashes.
questions.realWorldExample: The Rijndael cipher was created by Belgian cryptographers Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen.

questions.prompt: How many rounds are performed in AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256 respectively?
questions.explanation: AES uses 10 rounds for 128-bit keys, 12 rounds for 192-bit keys, and 14 rounds for 256-bit keys.
wrongExplanations: 16 rounds was used by DES.
These numbers do not match NIST FIPS 197 standards.
5 rounds would be vulnerable to cryptanalysis.
questions.realWorldExample: NIST selected Rijndael after a 3-year international competition evaluating security, efficiency, and hardware performance.

questions.prompt: Which transformation in an AES round provides NON-LINEAR CONFUSION?
questions.explanation: SubBytes substitutes each byte with an S-box derived from multiplicative inverse in GF(2^8) combined with an affine transformation.
wrongExplanations: Correct! SubBytes provides non-linear substitution.
ShiftRows provides diffusion by rotating rows.
MixColumns provides diffusion by mixing column matrix vectors.
AddRoundKey is linear bitwise XOR.
questions.realWorldExample: AES hardware acceleration instructions (AES-NI) execute SubBytes and MixColumns in a single CPU clock cycle.

questions.prompt: In the ShiftRows step of AES, how many bytes are cyclically shifted to the left in row 0, row 1, row 2, and row 3?
options: Row 0 shifts 0; Row 1 shifts 1; Row 2 shifts 2; Row 3 shifts 3
Row 0 shifts 1; Row 1 shifts 2; Row 2 shifts 3; Row 3 shifts 4
questions.explanation: Row 0 is not shifted. Row 1 rotates left by 1 byte. Row 2 rotates left by 2 bytes. Row 3 rotates left by 3 bytes.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Row 0: 0, Row 1: 1, Row 2: 2, Row 3: 3 bytes.
Shifting uniformly would not disperse byte positions across columns.
Row 0 must stay aligned for diffusion across multiple rounds.
Rows shift on every round.
questions.realWorldExample: Combined with MixColumns, ShiftRows ensures that after 4 rounds, every ciphertext bit depends on every plaintext bit.

questions.prompt: Why is the MixColumns step omitted in the final round of AES?
options: To make the decryption process architecturally symmetrical and faster
Because the computer runs out of memory
MixColumns produces errors on the 10th round
questions.explanation: Omitting MixColumns in the final round allows inverse AES decryption to mirror encryption without requiring extra round overhead.
wrongExplanations: Correct! It aligns encryption and decryption structures.
Memory usage in AES is tiny (under 1 KB for S-box tables).
MixColumns is mathematically sound across all rounds.
The key schedule produces round keys for all rounds.
questions.realWorldExample: Decryption reverses operations: InvShiftRows, InvSubBytes, InvAddRoundKey, InvMixColumns.

questions.prompt: What mathematical operation is executed during the AddRoundKey step?
options: Bitwise XOR between the 128-bit state matrix and the 128-bit round subkey
questions.explanation: AddRoundKey performs a simple, fast bitwise XOR between each byte of the state matrix and the corresponding byte of the expanded round key.
wrongExplanations: Correct! AddRoundKey is an XOR operation.
Exponentiation is used in RSA, not AES.
Floating point math is never used in block ciphers.
Substitution occurs in SubBytes.
questions.realWorldExample: AES Key Expansion generates (Nr + 1) round keys using RotWord, SubWord, and Rcon constants.

ashRecap: AES turns 16 bytes into an unbreakable dance: SubBytes swaps, ShiftRows slides, MixColumns blends, and AddRoundKey locks it in with the key!
